newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ANALYSTS SEE MANY MERGERS INVOLVING DUTCH INSURERS.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS SEE MANY MERGERS INVOLVING DUTCH INSURERS.

text.p: ING Groep is likely to unveil a big acquisition in the United States or Europe this year as part of another wave of mergers among Dutch insurers, analysts said.
They also said Aegon, which stunned market players by announcing a multi-billion purchase at the finish of 1996, would continue making acquisitions.
Aegon said last week it was buying Providian Corp's insurance activities, the biggest U.S. life insurance purchase to date and the biggest U.S. acquisition by a Dutch company.
"They all have ongoing acquisition plans," said Tom Bennett of Paribas, when asked about merger possibilities for listed Dutch insurers ING, Aegon, Fortis Amev and Stad Rotterdam.
"I expect some surprises from Fortis Amev," Bennet said. "Mostly in Europe, but the U.S. is also possible."
"The insurance industry, like other industries have done, shows a tendecy towards coagulation," said Tom Muller of NIBStrating Securities.
"It is difficult to predict whom will merge with whom. But the map (of insurance companies) will look quite different in about five years time," Muller said.
Muller sees three to five companies emerging as leaders in the European insurance market in the years to come.
He said Allianz of Germany and the merging French groups UAP and AXA were top European players in the world of insurance.
"Players in Great Britain are still somewhat divided," he said, adding that Commercial Union was big but did not belong at the top.
"ING could settle in the top-league later," Muller said. "But then, they should come up with a big alliance."
He mentioned a merger between ING and Swiss Winterthur as favourable chance. "But, a merger with a U.S. insurer would be even more likely," Muller said.
Dutch insurers have undergone three earlier merger waves. In the 1960s medium sized companies merged to defray the costs of introducing expensive computer systems.
In the 1970s insurance businesses mushroomed in size through acquisitions to increase the volume of their business and boost efficiency. Mergers became more international, crossing borders.
In the third wave in the late 1980s and early 1990s, insurers became even bigger.
They saw margins squeezed as clients became more demanding and they had to introduce new products.
This was also the time when insurers started linking up with banks and insurers became more international.
It was during this last big wave that insurer Nationale-Nederlanden and NMB Postbank merged to become ING.
Ago and Ennia had become Aegon about ten years earlier.
Dutch Amev, which had already acquired Dutch bank VSB, started an alliance with Belgian AG about six years ago, to become Fortis .
Spreading risks, increasing volumes to be more compatible and increase profitability after a good acquisition were the main reasons for the next concentration-wave, analysts said.
They said medium-sized Stad Rotterdam could stay independent as long it concentrated on the Dutch market.
"Stad Rotterdam is likely to stay a local operation," said Bennett of Paribas. "Although it could also be a nice acquisition for Fortis."
Fortis, currently digesting its latest acquisition -- merchant bank MeesPierson -- was also interested in upping its stake in Belgian ASLK by at least another 25 percent.
This stake is likely to be for sale later this year.
"But, Fortis has to expand even further," said NIBStrating's Muller.
He said plenty of acquisitions within the financial world were expected within the next few years.
"The concentration wave is going to be even more impressive if the U.S. changes its law, which would make it possible for banks and insurers to unite," said Muller.
"I expect this should be possible within one-and-a-half year."
Muller said this would open the door for the biggest Dutch bank ABN AMRO and insurer Aegon to merge. Rumours of such a move have always been played down by the two.
Muller sees it as a possibility as soon as the United States changes its law: "The combine of ABN AMRO and Aegon is starting to look like something," Muller added.
